newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto demands say in IMF terms for Pakistan loan.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto demands say in IMF terms for Pakistan loan.

text.p: Ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto has demanded that any agreement on an IMF restructuring loan being negotiated by Pakistan's caretaker government be approved by top political parties, her party said on Monday.

It released a trenchant letter from Bhutto to President Farooq Leghari saying the caretaker government he installed after dismissing her government earlier this month had no right to negotiate such loans.

"In any democratic system, long term pledges on matters of vital economic importance should only be made by a duly elected political government, responsible to the legislature and the people," she wrote.

The letter stopped short of saying she would disown the deal if the Supreme Court ruled that her government was deposed unconstitutionally, as she has asked it to, or her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) won elections scheduled for February.

An International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission that visited Pakistan after Bhutto was dismissed on charges of corruption and incompetence, accusations she vehemently denies, agreed to recommend the reactivation of a $600 million standby loan.
The deal, which the IMF board is expected to approve by mid-December, would involve the swift release of two tranches of $80 million to shore up Pakistan's low foreign reserves.
Leghari said last week Pakistan's liquid foreign reserves touched a year-low of $570 million on October 31 before rising to $630 million a week later.

He said the caretaker government aimed to move that figure up to $1 billion by the end of December despite debt repayments of $500 million due next month and a trade gap that widened from $415 million in September to $443 million in October.
Leghari also said the IMF had agreed to start talks on an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) and that agreement might be possible before the elections.
Bhutto was particularly incensed by that statement by her former ally, whom she has frequently criticised since being bundled out of office.

"Mr President, you are well aware that an agreement on ESAF binds the government to a three-year economic programme and involves numerous commitments on taxation, monetary policy, exchange rate, trade regime and other economic issues," she wrote.
"Such vital and sensitive decisions should be taken only by a duly elected government responsible to the people through the legislative and electoral process," she said.

Bhutto said the People's Democratic Front (PDF), a PPP-led alliance, and the Pakistan Muslim League of her chief political foe, former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, must agree to the conditions for a Structural Adjustment Loan.

"If the national interest demands that an agreement be signed by the IMF, you will have to take the PDF and the Muslim League (Nawaz) into confidence and get our agreement to any new conditions," she said.
"The nation demands to know what conditionalities you are discussing and promising without its consent or consent of its elected representatives."
There was no immediate comment from the president's office on the letter.
